chapters.title: Chapter 1: Getting Started with Python
chapters.goal: Set up Copilot and AI tooling to build your first application and then learn the core concepts and syntax so you can understand it fully.

examples.title: Hello World
examples.description: Write a simple Hello World program in Python to get started.
examples.prompt: Write a Hello World app

explanation.summary: This program displays the text "Hello, World!" on the screen. It is the traditional first program in any language, and proves that Python is installed and running correctly.

lines.text: print is a built-in function: you write its name, then parentheses holding the value you want it to handle. Python ships with print already defined, so nothing needs to be imported or set up first.

The quotation marks turn Hello, World! into a string, which is Python's word for a piece of text. Without them Python would read those words as names of things and complain that it has never heard of them.

The quotes mark where the text begins and ends and are not part of the output, so what appears on screen is Hello, World! and then a new line. A whole Python program can be one line long; there is no surrounding class or main function to declare.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Core Concepts
chapters.goal: Generate applications with prompts that use core Python concepts and learn how the code works with illustrated examples of Python core concepts.

examples.title: Basket of Fruits
examples.description: Create a program that manages a basket of fruits using variables and basic operations.
examples.prompt: Write a six line program with three baskets for apples, oranges, and bananas.

explanation.summary: This program makes three variables to hold how many apples, oranges, and bananas you have, then prints each count to the console.

lines.text: The equals sign is not a question about equality; it puts the value 5 into a basket named apples. The name goes on the left, the value you are storing goes on the right.
Each basket holds its own value independently, so creating a third variable does not disturb the first two.
The quoted text is printed literally, while apples without quotes prints the value stored inside it. Writing "apples" here would print the word rather than the number 5.
Passing two things to print separated by a comma puts them on one line with a space between them, which is why the label and the count read naturally together.

examples.title: Add Three Numbers
examples.description: Create a program that adds three numbers and prints the result.
examples.prompt: Write a program that adds 3 numbers and prints the result
response: # Add three numbers and print the result
# You can change these numbers as needed

explanation.summary: This program stores three numbers in variables, adds them together into a fourth variable, and prints the total. It is a first look at how a program holds values and combines them.

lines.code: # Add three numbers and print the result
lines.text: A comment is a note for people reading the code; Python ignores every line that starts with #, so it costs nothing to say what the program is for.
The = sign is an assignment, not a claim of equality: it puts the value 5 into a variable named num1 so the rest of the program can refer to it by name.

Python works out the right-hand side first, adding the three stored values, and only then stores the answer in result. Naming the total instead of adding inside the print keeps the calculation and the display separate.
Passing two things to print, separated by a comma, makes Python print them side by side with a space between, so you get a label and the number without any string juggling.

examples.title: Average Apple and Orange Weight
examples.description: Compute and print the average weight of an apple and an orange (in pounds).
examples.prompt: Write a program that adds the average weight of an apple and an orange in pounds
response: # Average weight of an apple (in pounds)
# Average weight of an orange (in pounds)
# Calculate the average of the two weights
print("The average weight of an apple and an orange is", average_weight, "pounds.")

explanation.summary: This program stores the average weight of an apple and an orange as decimal numbers, averages the two values, and prints the result in a sentence.

lines.text: A number written with a decimal point is a float, Python's type for fractional values, which is what you need for a weight in pounds rather than a whole count.

The parentheses matter: they force the addition to happen first, so the sum is divided by 2. Without them, Python's order of operations would divide only orange_weight by 2 and give a different answer.
Note that the prompt asked to add the two weights while the code averages them; when your description is loose, the AI picks one reading, so read the result before trusting it.

lines.code: print("The average weight of an apple and an orange is", average_weight, "pounds.")
lines.text: Passing print several arguments separated by commas lets you mix text with a number directly, and Python puts a single space between each piece automatically.

examples.title: Shopping Cart Items
examples.description: List items in a shopping cart using string concatenation.
examples.prompt: I have three items in my shopping cart. Use string concatenation to list them.
response: # List items in a shopping cart using string concatenation

explanation.summary: This program stores three shopping-cart items in variables and joins them into one readable line using the + operator, then prints the result.

lines.text: Each item is a string value held in its own variable, so the text lives in one place and the joining logic below can refer to it by name.

The + operator on strings means concatenation, not addition: it glues the pieces together end to end. The ", " in between is a literal separator, and the space inside the quotes is what keeps the items from running together.
Building the sentence with concatenation lets you reuse cart_list wherever it is needed, rather than repeating the three item names in the print call.

examples.title: Convert String to Uppercase
examples.description: Convert the string 'i lOvE pUpPiEs' to uppercase using Python's string methods.
examples.prompt: Convert the string "i lOvE pUpPiEs" to uppercase

explanation.summary: This program takes a string with a jumble of capital and lowercase letters and prints an all-capitals version of it using Python's built-in `upper()` method.

lines.text: The quotes are what make this a string, and Python keeps the letters exactly as typed, mixed cases and all, until you ask for something different.

`upper()` is a method that belongs to the string itself, which is why it is written after a dot on `text`. It returns a brand-new uppercase string rather than changing `text`, so the result has to be stored in a variable to be of any use.
Printing the new variable shows I LOVE PUPPIES; printing `text` here instead would still give the original mixed-case version, since strings in Python cannot be modified in place.

examples.title: Print Item Price
examples.description: Print the price of a specified item using an f-string and string concatenation.

prompts.prompt: Print the price of a specified item using an f string

explanation.summary: This short program stores an item name and its price in two variables, then uses an f-string to build one sentence that includes both values.

lines.text: A number written with a decimal point is a float, so Python stores 19.99 as a numeric value you could do arithmetic with, not as text.

The f before the opening quote marks this as an f-string: Python replaces each name in braces with that variable's value. Without the f, the output would contain the literal characters {item} and {price}.

The dollar sign here is just an ordinary character in the text; only the braces are special. Note also that the float prints as 19.99 exactly as typed — if you wanted a guaranteed two decimal places, you would ask for {price:.2f}.

prompts.prompt: Print the price of a specified item using string concatenation
response: print("The price of the " + item + " is $" + str(price))

explanation.summary: This program stores an item's name and its price in two variables, then joins them into one sentence with the + operator and prints it. Because price is a number, it has to be converted to text before it can be glued to the rest of the message.

lines.text: A number with a decimal point is a float, a separate type from the string in the line above. Note that there are no quotes here: 19.99 is a value you could do arithmetic with, while "19.99" would just be text.

lines.code: print("The price of the " + item + " is $" + str(price))
lines.text: The + operator between strings is concatenation: it joins pieces end to end rather than adding them. The spaces inside the quotes matter, since Python adds none of its own, and leaving them out would produce "The price of thebook".

lines.code: print("The price of the " + item + " is $" + str(price))
lines.text: str(price) converts the float into its string form so it can be concatenated. Without it Python raises a TypeError, because it refuses to guess whether + between a string and a number means joining or adding.

examples.title: Ask About the Weather
examples.description: Write and print a simple Boolean statement indicating if it is sunny today.
examples.prompt: Write a simple Boolean statement about the weather and print it

explanation.summary: This program stores a Boolean value \u2014 one of Python's two truth values \u2014 in a variable and prints it alongside a question. It is the smallest possible demonstration of the bool type.

lines.text: True is a Boolean value, not text: it is written with a capital T and no quotation marks. Writing "True" instead would store a string, and Python would treat it as a completely different kind of data.
Naming Boolean variables as yes-or-no questions, like is_sunny or has_paid, makes later code such as if is_sunny: read almost like English.
Passing print two arguments separated by a comma lets it show a piece of text and the value of a variable together, inserting a single space between them for you.

examples.title: Name and Greeting
examples.description: Ask the user for their name and print a greeting.
examples.prompt: Ask for the user's name and print it

explanation.summary: This program asks you to type your name in the terminal, then greets you using whatever you typed. It is the simplest example of a program whose output changes depending on what the user enters.

lines.text: The text inside input() is the prompt shown in the terminal, and the program pauses here until you type something and press Enter. Whatever you typed is then stored in the variable name.
The f before the quotes marks this as an f-string, so {name} is replaced by the value the user entered rather than printed literally. This is how the output changes from one run to the next.

examples.title: Pet Type and Name
examples.description: Ask for the type and name of the user's pet and output it.
examples.prompt: Ask for a pet's type and name, and output it
response: pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ")
pet_name = input("What is your pet's name? ")

explanation.summary: This program asks two questions in a row — what kind of pet you have and what it's called — and then prints a personalized sentence using both answers.

lines.code: pet_type = input("What type of pet do you have? ")
lines.text: A program is not limited to a single input; each call to input() pauses for one answer, and storing that answer in its own variable is what lets you collect several pieces of information.

lines.code: pet_name = input("What is your pet's name? ")
lines.text: The second question runs only after the first answer is entered, so the order of the prompts on screen is exactly the order of these lines. Note the apostrophe in "pet's" sits safely inside double quotes.
The f before the quote makes this an f-string, so both variable names in braces are replaced by what the user typed, and the rest of the sentence is printed literally.

examples.title: Treat Calorie Calculator
examples.description: Get how many treats a dog ate, and how many calories are in each treat. Calculate calorie consumption.
examples.prompt: Get how many treats a dog ate, and how many calories are in each treat. Calculate calorie consumption.
response: # Get user input for number of treats and calories per treat
num_treats = int(input("How many treats did the dog eat? "))
calories_per_treat = float(input("How many calories are in each treat? "))

explanation.summary: This program asks how many treats a dog ate and how many calories each treat has, then multiplies the two to report the total calories consumed. It shows typecasting text input into numbers so arithmetic works.

lines.code: num_treats = int(input("How many treats did the dog eat? "))
lines.text: A count of treats is a whole number, so the text coming back from input() is wrapped in int() before it is stored. If the reader types something that is not a number, the conversion fails and the program stops with an error.

lines.code: calories_per_treat = float(input("How many calories are in each treat? "))
lines.text: Calorie counts are not always whole, so this one is typecast with float() instead, which accepts decimals like 35.5.
Multiplication only makes sense here because both values were typecast first; multiplying the raw strings would have repeated text rather than done arithmetic.
The f-string drops the calculated total into the sentence. Because one value was a float, the result prints with a decimal point, as in 105.0.

examples.title: Data Types
examples.prompt: Write an eight line program to print attributes of a giraffe using basic data types.

explanation.summary: This program stores seven facts about a giraffe in variables, each using the data type that fits the fact, then prints them all as a tidy list of labelled lines.

lines.text:
Text goes in quotes, making this a string 
ever treated as a word rather than a number.
A measurement with a fractional part needs a float; the variable name records the unit so the number is never ambiguous.
A yes-or-no fact is a Boolean, and Python spells its two values `True` and `False` with a capital letter — lowercase `false` would be an error.
Whole counts like speed, spots, and years are integers; there is no need for a decimal point when nothing is ever half a spot.
The `f` before the quote lets each `{variable}` be swapped for its value, and each `\n` starts a new line, so one print statement produces Samantha's whole notebook page.

examples.title: Math
examples.prompt: Write a Python program that adds up the number of feet for a penguin, a panda, and a hippo.
response: # Define the number of feet for each animal

explanation.summary: This program stores the number of feet for a penguin, a panda, and a hippo in three variables, adds them together, and prints each animal's count along with the total.

lines.text: Each animal's foot count gets its own named variable, so the program reads like the problem Samantha described instead of a bare list of numbers.
The addition happens on the values stored in the variables, not on typed-in numbers, so changing an animal's count above automatically changes the total here.
The f before the quotes marks this as an f-string, and anything inside the curly braces is replaced by the variable's value when the line runs.
This is the answer Samantha actually wanted: ten feet means ten shoes to design.

examples.title: Pet Fetch
examples.prompt: Write a 5 line program to calculate the number of balls thrown. Take user input for the number of balls the dog retrieved, the number of balls the cat retrieved, and the number of balls that never got retrieved.
response: Enter number of balls dog retrieved: 8
Enter number of balls cat retrieved: 2
Enter number of balls never retrieved: 3

explanation.summary: This program asks for three counts — balls the dog brought back, balls the cat brought back, and balls that were never retrieved — and adds them together to report how many balls were thrown in total. What the book shows is a sample run: the numbers after each colon are what the reader typed in.

lines.code: Enter number of balls dog retrieved: 8
lines.text: The text up to the colon is the prompt the program displays; the 8 is typed by the person running it and is read in as a string, so it must be converted with int() before it can be added.

lines.code: Enter number of balls cat retrieved: 2
lines.text: A second input call collects the cat's tally, stored in its own variable so the three counts stay separate.

lines.code: Enter number of balls never retrieved: 3
lines.text: Balls that were thrown but never came back still count toward the total, which is why this third number is collected.
The three numbers are summed with + and printed; because they were converted to integers, 8 + 2 + 3 gives 13 rather than the joined text "823".

files.content:
dog = int(input("Enter number of balls dog retrieved: "))
cat = int(input("Enter number of balls cat retrieved: "))
lost = int(input("Enter number of balls never retrieved: "))
total = dog + cat + lost

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Loops and Flow Control
chapters.goal: Build applications with more complex logic using Python control structures.

examples.title: Temperature Hat Check
examples.description: This code asks the user the temperature, then uses an if statement to determine whether they need a hat. The program is then modified to include an else statement that tells you when you don't need a hat, and finally an elif conditional for sunscreen when it's too hot.

prompts.prompt: Write a 3 line program that tells you to wear a hat if the temperature is too low.

explanation.summary: This three-line program asks you for the current temperature and tells you to wear a hat when it is below 10°C. It is your first program that makes a decision instead of running every line no matter what.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float() converts what was typed into a number that can be compared against 10; without the conversion, comparing text to a number would fail.
This is the decision itself: the condition after if is either true or false, and the colon marks the start of the block that runs only when it is true.
The indentation is what puts this line inside the if. Python uses spacing rather than braces to show which lines belong to the decision.
Enter 15 and the program prints nothing at all, which looks broken to a user. That silence is the reason the next step is to add an else branch.

prompts.prompt: Modify this code to also tell you when not to wear a hat.

explanation.summary: This program asks for the current temperature and gives one of two pieces of advice: wear a hat when it is below 10 degrees, and no hat when it is not. It is the starting point for a decision that will later grow a third branch with elif.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float() converts what was typed into a number that can be compared with 10. Without that conversion, Python would refuse to compare a string to a number.
The condition is a question with a yes-or-no answer, and the colon plus the indented line beneath it marks off the code that runs only when the answer is yes.
The four spaces of indentation are what put this line inside the if. Python uses indentation, not braces, to decide which lines belong to a block.
else is the catch-all for every temperature that is not below 10, which is the piece this exercise asks you to add. Because exactly one of the two branches runs, the program always says something.

prompts.prompt: Use an elif to tell you if you need to wear sunscreen because it's too hot

explanation.summary: This program asks for a temperature and gives clothing advice, using an elif branch to catch hot weather as well as cold. Only one of the three messages ever prints.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so float() converts what was typed into a decimal number that can be compared against 10 and 30.
Python checks this condition first; if it is true, the cold-weather message prints and the rest of the chain is skipped entirely.
elif is short for "else if," and it lets you add a second question to the same if statement — it is only asked when the first condition turned out false.
The else branch is the catch-all for anything neither condition matched, which here means a comfortable temperature between 10 and 30.

examples.title: Dessert Recommendation with Nested Ifs
examples.description: Nested if loop program that recommends a dessert based on the weather and liking chocolate.
examples.prompt: Write a 12 line program with nested ifs to decide what dessert you should have based on whether it is hot outside and whether you like chocolate.

explanation.summary: This program asks two yes/no questions and recommends one of four desserts, using an if statement placed inside another if statement to combine the two answers.

lines.text: input always hands back text, so .strip() removes any stray spaces or the newline and .lower() turns "Y" into "y" 	ing only has to be compared against one form.
This is the outer decision, and it splits the program into the hot-day world and the cool-day world before the chocolate question is even considered.
The extra level of indentation is what makes this a nested decision: it is only reached when the outer condition was true, so it decides between the two hot-day desserts.
This else lines up with the outer if, not the inner one, so it opens the cool-day branch that holds its own complete if/else pair.
Every one of the four paths assigns dessert, so by the time this line runs the name is guaranteed to exist; leaving one branch out would crash here.

examples.title: Hello Three Times
examples.description: Using a for loop to print "Hello" three times.
examples.prompt: Write a program that says hello three times.

explanation.summary: This program prints the word "Hello" three times using a for loop instead of three separate print statements.

lines.text: This is the loop's instruction to repeat the indented code three times. Changing the 3 to 100 would print "Hello" a hundred times, which is where loops start saving you real work.
The variable i holds the current count on each pass, starting at 0. This program never uses i, but the loop still needs somewhere to keep track of where it is.
The indentation is what puts this line inside the loop. Without those spaces, Python would treat it as code that comes after the loop and print "Hello" only once.

examples.title: Count from 1 to 5
examples.description: For loop that counts from 1 to 5.
examples.prompt: Write a short program that counts from 1 to 5

explanation.summary: This two-line program prints the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, each on its own line. It uses a for loop with range() to walk through a sequence of numbers instead of writing five separate print statements.

lines.text: range(1, 6) produces the numbers starting at 1 and stopping just before 6, so the loop runs five times. The end value is not included, which is why counting to 5 needs a 6 here — this is the single most common off-by-one mistake beginners make.
The variable i is the loop variable: on each pass through the loop Python assigns it the next number in the range, so its value changes automatically without you writing i = i + 1.

The indentation is what puts this line inside the loop body, so it is what gets repeated. Remove the indentation and Python would report an error, because a for statement must be followed by an indented block.

examples.title: Count Down from 5 to 1
examples.description: For loop with three arguments that counts down.
examples.prompt: Write a short program that counts from 5 to 1.

explanation.summary: This program counts backwards, printing 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 on separate lines. It uses the three-argument form of `range` to walk a sequence in reverse.

lines.text: The three numbers are the start, the stop, and the step: begin at 5, keep going while the value is above 0, and subtract 1 each time. Without the `-1` step, `range` counts upward and produces nothing at all here, since 5 is already past 0.
The stop value is still excluded, so writing 0 is what makes the countdown end at 1. A beginner who writes `range(5, 1, -1)` gets 5, 4, 3, 2 and wonders where the 1 went.
The indentation is what puts this line inside the loop, so it runs once per pass with `i` holding the current count.

examples.title: Multiplication Table with Nested Loops
examples.description: Nested for loop multiplication table program.
examples.prompt: Use nested loops to output the times table up to 10 without headings.

explanation.summary: This program prints the multiplication table from 1×1 up to 10×10 as a neat grid of numbers. It uses one for loop inside another so that every row's ten columns get filled in before moving on to the next row.

lines.text: The outer loop runs ten times, once per row of the table, and `i` holds the row number. Remember that `range(1, 11)` stops before 11, so this gives you 1 through 10.
The inner loop is the nested one: it runs its full ten times for every single pass of the outer loop, which is what produces 100 numbers rather than 10.

The `:3` inside the f-string pads each product to three characters wide so the columns line up even when the numbers go from one digit to three. The `end=' '` replaces the usual newline with a space, keeping the whole row on one line.
This bare `print()` sits in the outer loop, not the inner one, so it fires once per row to end the line and start the next. Without it every number would run together on a single endless line.

examples.title: Loop Over Musical Scale
examples.description: For loop that loops over the "letters" string.
examples.prompt: Write a program that stores the musical letters in a string and then prints them one per line.

explanation.summary: This program stores the seven letters of the musical scale in a single string and prints each one on its own line. It shows that a for loop can walk through the characters of a string, not just a range of numbers.

lines.text: The whole musical scale lives in one string, seven characters long. Python treats a string as a sequence of characters, which is exactly what makes it loopable.

Here the loop is given a string instead of a range, so `letter` holds one character at a time: first "A", then "B", and so on through "G". Nothing tells the loop to stop after seven turns — it runs out when the string runs out.
Because print adds a newline each time it is called, and it is called once per turn of the loop, the seven notes come out one per line.

examples.title: Feed Parrot Until Full
examples.description: While loop program for feeding a parrot.
examples.prompt: Write an 8 line program where you keep feeding the parrot seeds until it is full.
response: print(f"Parrot needs {capacity} seeds to be full.")

explanation.summary: This program feeds Bruno's parrot seeds a handful at a time, asking you how many to give and keeping a running total, and it stops as soon as the parrot has had enough.

lines.text: The loop keeps going as long as the running total is still short of the parrot's capacity, so the number of feedings is decided by what you type rather than fixed in advance.
Whatever you type arrives as text, so int() converts it to a number before it can be added; the prompt recalculates the remaining amount each time round the loop.
max(0, feed) treats a negative entry as zero, so nobody can take seeds back out of the parrot and stall the loop forever.
These two names look almost identical but mean different things: feed is the handful you just gave, while fed is everything the parrot has eaten so far.
Because this line sits outside the loop with no indentation, it runs once at the end, after the condition finally fails.

examples.title: Count to 10 Skip Multiples of 3
examples.description: Program which counts to 10 and uses a continue to skip multiples of 3.
examples.prompt: Write a while loop that prints numbers from 1 to 10, but skips every multiple of 3.

explanation.summary: This program counts from 1 to 10 with a while loop, but skips printing any number that divides evenly by 3, so you see 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10.

lines.text: The modulo operator gives the remainder of a division, so a remainder of zero means `i` is an exact multiple of 3 and should be skipped.

This increment has to happen before `continue`, because `continue` jumps straight back to the condition and any line below it would never run. Forget this one and `i` stays at 3 forever, giving an infinite loop.
The normal path needs its own increment as well, since the loop only advances when you move the counter yourself.
`continue` abandons the rest of this pass through the loop and starts the next one, which is how the multiples of 3 get skipped instead of printed.

examples.title: Count Until User Says Stop
examples.description: Number counter program that will stop counting when the user says stop.
examples.prompt: Write a 9 line program that keeps counting until the user says stop.
response: s = input("Press Enter to continue or type stop: ")

explanation.summary: This program counts upward one number at a time, pausing after each one to ask the user whether to continue, and stops only when the user types "stop". It shows a loop whose ending is decided by the person at the keyboard rather than by a fixed count.

lines.text: A condition that is always true means the loop never ends on its own; the only way out is the break inside the body. This is the shape you reach for when you cannot know in advance how many times the loop should run.

lines.code: s = input("Press Enter to continue or type stop: ")
lines.text: The loop pauses here on every pass, which is what lets the user, rather than a counter, decide when the program finishes. Pressing Enter alone hands back an empty string, which is not the stop word, so counting continues.

Calling strip removes stray spaces and the newline, and lower folds capitals down, so STOP and ' Stop ' are all accepted. Comparing raw input would reject anything but a perfectly typed lowercase word.
The break statement is the exit door out of an infinite loop; it abandons the loop immediately and continues with whatever follows it.
Because this sits after the break, it only runs when the user chose to continue, so the number shown next time is one higher.

examples.title: If/Else with Booleans
examples.prompt: Modify the program with a yes/no question to ask the user if they would like to use Celsius

explanation.summary: This program asks whether you prefer Celsius, stores that answer as a True/False value, then reads a temperature and gives clothing advice. If you chose Fahrenheit, it converts your number to Celsius first so the comparisons still make sense.

lines.text: The comparison `== "yes"` produces a Boolean, so `use_celsius` holds True or False rather than the text the user typed. Calling `.strip()` removes stray spaces and `.lower()` folds "YES" or "Yes" down to "yes", so small differences in typing still count as agreement; anything else, including "no", makes it False.
A Boolean variable can be tested on its own — there is no need to write `if use_celsius == True`, because the variable already is the answer to the question.
`input` always hands back text, so `float` is needed to turn "70" into a number you can do arithmetic and comparisons with.

The Fahrenheit reading is converted into Celsius and stored in `temp`, so the rest of the program only ever deals with one scale. This is why 70°F is treated as mild instead of triggering the sunscreen advice.
`elif` is only reached when the `if` above it was False, and the final `else` catches everything left over — every temperature between 10 and 30 lands there.

examples.title: While Loops
examples.prompt: Parrot needs 10 seeds to be full.

explanation.summary: This is the heart of the parrot-feeding program: a while loop that keeps asking you for seeds until the total the parrot has eaten reaches its capacity of 10.

lines.text: The loop's condition is checked before every pass, so feeding continues only while the running total is still short of capacity; once fed reaches 10 the loop ends on its own without any counter to manage.
Because `input` always hands back text, `int` converts what you typed into a number you can add up, and the prompt recomputes `capacity-fed` each time so it always reflects how much room is left.
`max(0, feed)` quietly guards against a negative entry: the parrot cannot un-eat its food, so anything below zero contributes nothing to the total.
The two variables are easy to confuse: `feed` is the amount from this one round, while `fed` is the running total that the loop condition watches.

examples.title: Counting Down and For Loop Syntax
examples.prompt: Write a short rocket program that counts from 5 to 1.

explanation.summary: This program counts down from 5 to 1, pausing one second between each number, then announces blastoff. It shows how a for loop can run backward using a third argument to range.

lines.text: The time module is part of Python's standard library, and it gives us the sleep function used below to make the countdown feel like a real countdown.

The third argument, -1, is the step: instead of adding 1 each pass, the loop subtracts 1. Since the loop stops before reaching the second number, the stop value must be 0 for the countdown to include 1.
Pausing the program for one second on each pass is what stretches the five numbers over five seconds rather than printing them all instantly.
This line sits outside the loop, with no indentation, so it runs once after the countdown finishes rather than after every number.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Data Structures
chapters.goal: Learn the core Python data structures by building applications that demonstrate these concepts and learning from the illustrated explanations of these important concepts.

examples.title: Accessing and Modifying Lists
examples.prompt: Modify the list to include a Portuguese item that would be easy to buy in a grocery store. Use changing, adding, removing, then accessing at the end.
response: shopping_list[4] = "chouriço"  # Replace snacks with Portuguese sausage
shopping_list.append("pastéis de nata")  # Portuguese custard tarts

explanation.summary: This program takes Alex's birthday party shopping list and updates it with Portuguese groceries, using list operations to change, add, and remove items before printing the finished list.

lines.code: shopping_list[4] = "chouriço"  # Replace snacks with Portuguese sausage
lines.text: Lists are mutable, so assigning to a position overwrites whatever was stored there. Index 4 is the fifth item, because Python starts counting at 0.

lines.code: shopping_list.append("pastéis de nata")  # Portuguese custard tarts
lines.text: append adds a new item onto the end of the list, growing it by one; you never have to say how big the list should be in advance.
remove deletes by value rather than by position, so you name the item you want gone. If the item is not in the list, Python raises an error instead of quietly doing nothing.
A for loop walks through the list one item at a time, so the printed list always reflects the current contents no matter how many changes were made above.
A negative index counts backward from the end, so -1 is the final item. This is how you reach the last element without knowing the list's length.

examples.title: Iterating Over a List
examples.prompt: Write an 7 line roll call program that goes through a fixed list of students, asks if they are present, and prints the list of absentees.

explanation.summary: This program walks through a fixed list of student names, asks whether each one is present, and collects the names that were not answered "yes" so it can print the absentees at the end.

lines.text: An empty list is created up front so there is somewhere to collect names as the loop discovers them; you cannot append to a list that does not exist yet.
This is the same loop syntax used for strings in Chapter 3, but here each pass hands you one element of the list, so the variable student holds "Alice", then "Bob", and so on.
The f-string drops the current student's name into the question, and .lower() folds the reply to lowercase so "Yes" and "YES" are treated the same as "yes".
Anything other than "yes" counts as absent, so a blank reply or a typo lands the student on the list — a deliberate choice to keep the program short.
append adds the name to the end of the absentees list, growing it as the roll call proceeds rather than replacing what is already there.
This sits outside the loop, so it runs once after every student has been asked; printing a list shows it in Python's bracket notation.

examples.title: Sorting Lists
examples.prompt: Create a program that creates a list of fish types with some duplicates and sorts them alphabetically

explanation.summary: This program stores a fisherman's haul of fish names in a list, including a repeated "Salmon", and sorts the list alphabetically so identical catches end up next to each other.

lines.text: A list happily holds the same value twice, which is exactly what we want here: the two salmon are both recorded rather than one overwriting the other.

The built-in sort function does the ordering for us, so we never have to write comparison logic of our own. It rearranges this list in place instead of handing back a new one, which is why nothing is assigned to a variable here.
Printing the list after sorting shows the fish in alphabetical order, and the duplicate salmon appear side by side so the fisherman can spot them at a glance.

examples.title: Tuples
examples.prompt: Using only tuples, describe a car with different attributes.

explanation.summary: This program stores nine facts about one car in a single tuple and then prints a couple of those facts back out by their position. Because a car's make, model, and year never change, a tuple is a better fit than a list.

lines.text: The parentheses are what make this a tuple rather than a list. Once the closing parenthesis is reached, the contents are locked in for good — no item can be replaced, added, or removed.
A tuple has no field names, so the comment beside each item is the only record of what that position means. Keeping the order intact matters, because position is the only way back to a value.
One tuple can hold text, whole numbers, and decimals side by side; 2022 is stored as a number while the make and model are strings.

Items are pulled out by index, and counting starts at 0, so car[0] is the make and car[2] is the year. This is the same square-bracket access you used with lists — reading from a tuple is not restricted, only changing it.
The indexes can be used in any order you like, but you have to count positions by hand every time you want a value. That bookkeeping is exactly what unpacking, coming up next, removes.

examples.title: Unpacking Tuples
examples.prompt: Write a program that uses tuple unpacking for Sam's winter gear. Unpack his clothes into three categories: a hat, outerwear, and shoes.
response: # Unpack the tuple into three categories

explanation.summary: This program stores Sam's three winter clothing items in a tuple and then uses tuple unpacking to move each item into its own named variable, so the rest of the code can talk about a hat, outerwear, and shoes instead of positions.

lines.text: Sam's clothes start packed tightly together in a single tuple, where each item is only identified by its position in the parentheses.

This is the unpacking itself: one line hands out the three values in the tuple to three new variables, in order, so "Beanie" lands in hat and "Boots" lands in shoes. The number of variables on the left has to match the number of items in the tuple exactly, or Python raises a ValueError.
The f prefix here is harmless but unnecessary, since this string has no {} placeholders to fill in — a plain string would print the same heading.
Because the value now lives in a variable with an English name, the print statement reads like a sentence; compare this to writing winter_gear[0] and having to remember what position zero meant.

examples.title: Creating Dictionaries
examples.prompt: Create a dictionary for a fantasy world item shop containing a sword, a spell, and a potion, along with their price.

explanation.summary: This builds a dictionary named shop that holds Sally's three items paired with their prices. Each item name is a key, and the price stored alongside it is that key's value.

lines.text: The curly braces open a dictionary, which is Python's structure for storing data in pairs rather than in a plain sequence. Everything between this brace and the closing one is Sally's whole inventory.
The colon is what makes this a pair: "sword" is the key an adventurer would ask for, and 150 is the value Sally charges for it. The trailing comma separates this pair from the next one.

The last pair needs no comma after it, and its price is deliberately the cheapest so the beginning adventurer on a budget can afford one. Each key in a dictionary must be unique, which is exactly why every item can carry its own price.

The closing brace finishes the dictionary and the assignment, so shop now refers to all three pairs at once. Note that nothing is printed yet -- this exercise only builds the inventory, and looking a price up by name comes next.

examples.title: Storing Lists in Dictionaries
examples.prompt: Create a dictionary for student classes at a magic academy. Create lists of classes for Sally and four other students.

explanation.summary: This program builds a dictionary where each key is a student's name and each value is a list of that student's magic classes, then prints one tidy line per student. It shows how nesting a list inside a dictionary lets a single key hold many items.

lines.text: The value here is a list in square brackets, not a single string, which is what lifts the dictionary beyond one paired value per key. Sally's four classes stay in the order they were written.
The last entry takes no trailing comma before the closing brace, and the closing brace sits on its own line so the whole bulletin board reads as one block.
Each item from a dictionary comes out as a name-and-value pair, and listing two variables unpacks that pair in one step: student gets the key, classes gets the whole list.
join glues the list items into a single string separated by a comma and a space, which is far neater than printing the raw list with its brackets and quotes.

examples.title: Try/Except
examples.prompt: Ask for user input to share cupcakes among llamas. Handle errors accordingly
response: cupcakes = int(input("How many cupcakes do you have? "))
llamas = int(input("How many llamas are sharing the cupcakes? "))
print("Error: Please enter valid whole numbers for cupcakes and llamas.")
print("Error: You can't share cupcakes among zero llamas!")

explanation.summary: This program asks the user how many cupcakes and how many llamas there are, then divides them evenly. Instead of crashing on bad input, it catches the two errors that are likely and prints a friendly message.

lines.text: Everything that might go wrong lives inside the try block, so if any line in it fails, Python jumps straight to a matching except block instead of stopping the program.

lines.code: cupcakes = int(input("How many cupcakes do you have? "))
lines.text: The text typed by the user is always a string, so it must be typecast with int() before it can be used in arithmetic — and this is exactly the call that fails if the user types "three" or "2.5".
The :.2f inside the f-string rounds the result to two decimal places, which keeps the output readable when the division doesn't come out even.
A ValueError is what int() raises when the text isn't a whole number, so catching it turns a crash into a clear instruction to the user.
Except blocks can be chained so each kind of failure gets its own response; this one covers the case where the user enters zero llamas, which mathematics won't allow.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Functions
chapters.goal: Understand how to modularize applications using functions and lambdas to create more maintainable code.

examples.title: Single-Argument Functions
examples.prompt: Write a function to help Beepo the robot waiter roll up to the correct table and greet. The function should take one argument for the table number. Call the function three times.
response: """Beepo the robot waiter greets at the specified table."""
print(f"Beep boop! Rolling up to table {table_number}...")
print(f"Welcome to table {table_number}! How can I assist you today?")

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that sends Beepo the robot waiter to a table and greets the customers there, then calls it three times with three different table numbers.

lines.text: The `def` keyword defines the function, and `table_number` is its parameter \u2014 a placeholder that stands in for whichever table number is supplied when the function is called.

lines.code: """Beepo the robot waiter greets at the specified table."""
lines.text: A docstring is a short description placed as the first line inside a function, explaining in plain words what the function is for so anyone reading the code later knows its purpose.

lines.code: print(f"Beep boop! Rolling up to table {table_number}...")
lines.text: The body of the function is indented, and everything indented under `def` belongs to the function. The f-string drops the current value of `table_number` into the message, so the wording changes with each call.
Defining a function does nothing on its own; this call is what actually runs the body. The `1` is the argument, and it becomes the value of `table_number` for the duration of this call.
Three calls with three different arguments reuse the same four lines of logic, which is the point of a function \u2014 Beepo visits a different table each time without you rewriting the greeting.

examples.title: Multi-Argument Functions
examples.prompt: Create a function to help Beepo the robot waiter to deliver food to a table. The function should take two arguments: a food list and table number. Call the function twice.
response: """Helps Beepo the robot waiter deliver food to a table."""

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that takes two pieces of information at once \u2014 a list of food and a table number \u2014 and prints out Beepo's delivery for that table. Calling it twice with different arguments shows the same function doing the same job for two different orders.

lines.text: Two parameters, separated by a comma, let the function receive two pieces of information in one call. Their order matters: whatever you pass first becomes food_list, and whatever you pass second becomes table_number.

lines.code: """Helps Beepo the robot waiter deliver food to a table."""
lines.text: A docstring sits just inside the function and states in plain words what the function is for, so anyone reading the code later knows Beepo's job without tracing the lines.
A parameter can hold any type of data, including a whole list, so the function loops through the order and prints each item in turn no matter how many dishes were sent in.
The \n adds a blank line at the end, which keeps the two deliveries visually separated when the function runs more than once.
The list is written directly inside the parentheses as the first argument and the table number as the second, matching the order of the parameters in the definition.
Calling the same function a second time with different arguments is the whole point of writing a function: one set of instructions, reused for every order Beepo takes.

examples.title: Function Returns
examples.prompt: Create a function to help Beepo the robot waiter take payment from a numbered table according to the items ordered (everything costs $2). Call the function three times to collect money, put it in the cash register, and print the total.
response: """Collects payment from a table based on items ordered ($2 each)"""

explanation.summary: This program defines a function that works out what a table owes based on how many items they ordered, then calls it for three different tables and keeps a running total in a cash register variable.

lines.text: len() counts how many items are in the list that was passed in, and each one costs $2. Beepo never needs to know what the items actually are, only how many there were.
This hands the calculated amount back to the main program and ends the function immediately. Without it, the caller would receive None and there would be nothing to add up.
The register starts empty before any tables are visited, so that money can be added to it. Trying to add to a variable that does not exist yet is an error.
The returned amount is caught and added straight into the register. This is the point of a return value: had the result not been stored somewhere, it would simply disappear.
The \n prints a blank line first, separating the three table receipts from the final total. All three calls have finished by now, so the register holds the sum of them all.

examples.title: Playing High Card
examples.prompt: Use this generator to play one hand of high card.
response: deck = [(f'{rank} of {suit}', value) for suit in suits for value, rank in enumerate(ranks)]

explanation.summary: This program deals two cards from a shuffled deck \u2014 one for you, one for the computer \u2014 and declares whoever holds the higher card the winner. It reuses the card generator from earlier, now that each card carries a numeric value alongside its name.

lines.code: deck = [(f'{rank} of {suit}', value) for suit in suits for value, rank in enumerate(ranks)]
lines.text: Each card is now a pair: its printable name and a number for comparing. `enumerate(ranks)` hands back a position along with each rank, so '2' scores 0 and 'Ace' scores 12 \u2014 the exact ordering the game needs.
`yield` is what makes this a generator: the deck is handed out one card at a time, on request, instead of all at once. This is why the game can simply ask for the next card whenever a player draws.
Calling the generator function does not deal any cards yet; it creates the generator object that will produce them. Note that this `deck` is a separate variable from the list inside the function.

Each `next(deck)` draws one card, and the tuple on the left unpacks both cards into four named variables in a single step. Because the generator never repeats a card, the player and the computer cannot draw the same one.
This is a conditional expression: Python picks one of the three strings before `print` ever runs. Comparing the numeric ranks, not the card names, is what makes 'Ace' beat '10' correctly.

examples.title: Filter Function
examples.prompt: Create a list of goats and use filter to get the calmest ones.

explanation.summary: This program stores a herd of goats as a list of dictionaries, each with a name and a calm level, then uses filter with a lambda to keep only the goats calm enough to bring to the baby shower.

lines.text: Each goat is its own dictionary, so one entry can carry both the name and the calm level. Grouping related facts like this is what lets a single lambda inspect the calm level and still know which goat it belongs to.

filter works like map: you hand it a function and a list. The difference is that the lambda answers a true-or-false question about each goat, and only the goats that answer true survive into the new list.
The list() call around filter is required if you want a real list you can print or reuse. Without it you get a filter object that gives up its goats only once, as you loop over it.
Inside an f-string delimited by double quotes, the dictionary keys are written with single quotes. Reusing double quotes there would end the string early and break the line.

examples.title: Reduce Function
examples.prompt: Use reduce to calculate how many eggs a list of chickens laid in total. Then calculate how many muffins can be made from those eggs (1 egg per 6 muffins)
response: total_eggs = reduce(lambda total, chicken: total + chicken["eggs_laid"], chickens, 0)

explanation.summary: This program uses reduce to add up the eggs laid by each chicken in a list of dictionaries, then works out how many muffins that many eggs will make. It prints the egg total and the muffin count with f-strings.

lines.text: Unlike map and filter, reduce is not available by default, so it has to be imported from Python's functools library before you can use it.

lines.code: total_eggs = reduce(lambda total, chicken: total + chicken["eggs_laid"], chickens, 0)
lines.text: reduce combines a whole list down into one value, and takes three things: the function that does the combining, the list to walk through, and the value to start from. The lambda here has two parameters because reduce hands it the running total so far along with the next chicken.

lines.code: total_eggs = reduce(lambda total, chicken: total + chicken["eggs_laid"], chickens, 0)
lines.text: The starting value of 0 matters: Mary has no eggs collected before she begins, so the running total begins at zero. Notice too that there is no list() wrapped around this call, since reduce returns a single number rather than a sequence.
Because one egg is enough for six muffins, the egg total is multiplied by six to get the batch size Mary can bake.
The f before the quote lets you drop a variable straight into the text inside curly braces, so the number appears in the sentence rather than on a line of its own.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Object-Oriented Programming
chapters.goal: Learn object-oriented programming techniques that provide encapsulation and abstraction for building more complex applications.

examples.title: Classes and Attributes
examples.prompt: Create a robot pet class with the attributes name, battery, and mood. Then create three pets and print their attributes.

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class, a blueprint for creating robot pet objects that each carry a name, a battery level, and a mood. It then creates three distinct pets and prints each one's attributes.

lines.text: This is the constructor, a special method Python runs automatically whenever a new RobotPet is created. The arguments after self are the pieces of information you must supply about the pet.
The argument name only exists while the constructor runs; assigning it to self.name stores it on the pet object itself so it can be read back later. The same pattern saves battery and mood.

Calling the class like a function builds one pet in a single line, and the arguments are matched to the constructor's parameters in order. This is what makes creating many unique pets so much less work than writing a dictionary for each.
Dot notation reads an attribute back off a particular object, so pet1.name is Rover's name and never Sparky's. Each pet keeps its own separate copy of the three attributes.

examples.title: Methods
examples.prompt: Add a method that checks if the pet has enough energy for a walk with a duration you can set and check the animals to see if they can do a 30 minute walk.
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
# Check if pets can do a 30 minute walk

explanation.summary: This program adds a can_walk method to the RobotPet class, which reports whether a pet has enough battery for a walk of any length you ask about. Three pets are created and each is checked for a 30-minute walk.

lines.text: A method is a function that lives inside a class. Like __init__, its first parameter is self, so the method can look at the attributes of whichever pet it was called on; duration is the value you pass in when you call it.

This is the rule Frederick's shop uses: each minute of walking costs two ticks of battery. Because the duration arrives as a parameter, the same method answers the question for a 5-minute stroll or an hour-long hike.

The comparison itself evaluates to True or False, and return hands that answer back to whoever called the method. Nothing is printed here — a method that returns a value leaves the printing to the caller.
The \n is an escape sequence for a newline, so this prints a blank line before the heading and separates the two blocks of output.
Calling the method on pet1 with the dot means Rover is the self inside can_walk, so his own battery is the one checked. The returned True or False is dropped straight into the f-string.

examples.title: Encapsulation
examples.prompt: Use encapsulation to protect the battery attribute and ensure it doesn't go above 100 or below 0
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
"""Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""

explanation.summary: This version of RobotPet guards the battery attribute so it can never be set above 100 or below 0. The battery value is read and written through a property, and the setter clamps any out-of-range number to a safe level.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Even inside `__init__`, the assignment goes through the setter rather than storing the number raw, so a pet created with a bad battery value is corrected the moment it is built.
The `@property` decorator turns the method below it into the read path for `pet.battery`, so reading the attribute quietly calls a method instead of fetching a stored value.
The real value now lives in `_battery`, and the leading underscore is Python's convention for an internal attribute that code outside the class should leave alone.
This registers the write path, so every `pet.battery = ...` anywhere in the program is routed through the validation below and cannot bypass it.
These three branches are the whole point of the encapsulation: a negative charge becomes 0, anything over 100 becomes 100, and a sensible value is stored unchanged.
Try changing 85 to 120, or Beep's 45 to -40, and run the program again: the printed batteries come back as 100 and 0, which is how you prove the setter is doing its job.

examples.title: Encapsulation
examples.prompt: Test walk and charge methods on Rover
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
"""Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
# Test walk and charge methods on Rover
print(f"{pet1.name} doesn't have enough battery to walk {duration} minutes.")
print(f"{pet1.name} doesn't have enough battery to walk {duration} minutes.")

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet class whose battery level is guarded by a property setter, then puts Rover through two walks and a charge to show the guard at work. Walking costs 2% of battery per minute, and charging can never push the battery past 100%.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Even inside __init__, assigning to self.battery goes through the property setter rather than storing the value directly, so a pet can never be created with an impossible starting battery.

This decorator makes the method below run every time anything assigns to .battery, which is where the clamping to the 0-100 range happens. Everywhere else in the program you write plain assignment and the validation follows for free.
can_walk is a look-before-you-leap check: it reports whether the pet has the energy for the requested walk without changing anything.
This subtraction is really a read of the getter followed by an assignment through the setter, so the battery drains but can never fall below 0.
Asking can_walk first is what makes the second walk of 50 minutes get refused instead of silently draining Rover to nothing.
Rover is at 65% and asks for 40 more, which would be 105; the setter quietly caps him at 100, which is the whole point of protecting the attribute.

examples.title: Inheritance
examples.prompt: Add robot pet subclasses for a cat, bird, and dog. Then create one of each type. Finally, call each animal’s method.
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation

explanation.summary: This program reworks Frederick's RobotPet class into a family of pets: RobotCat, RobotBird, and RobotDog each inherit RobotPet's setup and battery protection, and each adds its own sound method. One of each is created and asked to speak.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery inside __init__ goes through the property setter rather than storing the number directly, so a pet cannot be born with an impossible battery level. Every subclass gets this checking for free.
The parent class in parentheses is what makes RobotCat a subclass: it inherits the __init__ and the battery property from RobotPet without repeating a line of them.
Each subclass adds only what makes it different. meow belongs to cats alone, so a RobotBird has no meow and calling one would be an error.
The method reaches self.name, an attribute the parent's __init__ set, showing that inherited attributes are fully available inside a subclass's own methods.
RobotCat defines no __init__ of its own, so Python uses the one it inherited, which is why the three arguments are still name, battery, and mood.
Each object answers with its own species' sound method, which is the payoff of inheritance: shared behaviour lives in one place, and only the differences are written three times.

examples.title: Calling Super Methods
examples.prompt: The talents should use the battery. Put this logic in the base class instead of performing a generic trick.
response: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
return f"{self.name} has no battery left and cannot perform!"
return f"{self.name} is low on battery and can barely perform..."
return f"{self.name} gracefully balances on two legs! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
return f"{self.name} mimics a beautiful melody! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
return f"{self.name} catches a frisbee in mid-air! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"

explanation.summary: Each robot pet's talent method now begins by asking its parent class whether the pet has enough battery to perform. The shared battery check lives once in RobotPet, and the three subclasses build their own tricks on top of it.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery inside __init__ goes through the property setter rather than storing the number directly, so a value passed in at creation time is clamped to the 0-100 range just like any later change.
The battery rule is written once, here in the base class, so all three pets share it. If the rule ever changes, there is a single place to change it.
When the battery is healthy, the base method deliberately returns nothing. Returning None is how this method says "no objection" and hands the decision back to the subclass.
super() reaches up to RobotPet and runs its version of show_talent, which the subclass would otherwise have replaced entirely. Writing RobotPet.show_talent(self) would do exactly the same thing.
A message string is truthy and None is falsy, so this one test decides whether to pass the parent's warning along or continue on to the trick.
The same call on each pet in the list produces a different trick, because Python looks up show_talent on the object's own class first.

examples.title: Composition
examples.prompt: Create a RobotPetShelter class that stores robot pet objects in a list that is encapsulated. Add methods to add a pet, show all pets, and find a pet by name. Then create some pets.

explanation.summary: This program builds a RobotPetShelter class that keeps its robot pets in a private list, with methods to add a pet, list every pet, and look one up by name. Three pets from the previous section are created, added to the shelter, and then Rex is found by name so his talent can be shown.

lines.text: The shelter's one attribute is the list that holds the pets, and the double underscore keeps it private so pets can only get in and out through the shelter's own methods.
An empty list is falsy, so this guard reports that the shelter is empty instead of returning a blank string.
type(pet).__name__ asks each object which class it came from, so a cat, a bird, and a dog each label themselves correctly with no extra work in the shelter.
Lowercasing both names makes the search case-insensitive, so "rex", "Rex", and "REX" all find the same pet.
When the loop finishes without a match, the method hands back None, which is why the main body tests the result before calling a method on it.
This is composition in action: the pet objects now live inside a shelter object rather than in a loose list beside the code.

files.content:
"""Sets up the robot pet classes from the previous section, then runs this program."""
import builtins
import contextlib
import io
import os
import runpy

# Load the pet classes quietly, so only the shelter program's output is shown.
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()):
    pets = runpy.run_path("robot_pets.py")

for name in ("RobotPet", "RobotCat", "RobotBird", "RobotDog"):
    setattr(builtins, name, pets[name])

here = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
for filename in sorted(os.listdir(here)):
    if filename.endswith(".py") and filename not in ("run_shelter.py", "robot_pets.py"):
        runpy.run_path(os.path.join(here, filename), run_name="__main__")
        break

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Unit Tests
chapters.goal: AI is a great assistant for unit testing. Learn how to apply AI to automatically write unit tests and assertions of your code.

examples.title: Assert
examples.prompt: Create a RobotPet class and a method that checks if the pet has enough battery to go on a walk.
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""

explanation.summary: This defines the RobotPet class from the robot pet shop, giving each pet a name, a battery level, and a mood, plus a can_walk method that works out whether the battery can cover a walk of a given length. Two pets are then created so there is something concrete to test.

lines.text: The initializer is what runs when you create a pet, and its three parameters become the pet's starting state. Every test you write later begins by choosing these values.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: This docstring records the rule the method is meant to follow, in minutes. When you ask the AI to generate tests, this sentence is what it uses to decide what correct behaviour looks like.
This is the pet shop's rule made concrete: robot pets spend 2 battery points for every minute of walking, so a 10-minute walk costs 20 points.
A comparison evaluates to True or False, so the method hands back a plain boolean rather than printing anything. That is exactly what an assert statement needs to check.
Creating a pet with a known battery level is what makes testing possible: because you chose 85, you can predict in advance which walks should be allowed and assert it.
A second pet with a much lower battery gives you a contrasting case, so your tests can confirm can_walk says no as well as yes.

examples.title: Assert
examples.prompt: Add two unit tests using assert to check if the pets can walk
response: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
assert rover.can_walk(30) == True, "Rover should be able to walk for 30 minutes"
assert beep.can_walk(30) == False, "Beep should not be able to walk for 30 minutes"

explanation.summary: This program defines a RobotPet whose can_walk method works out whether the pet's battery can cover a walk of a given length, then checks that method with two assert statements. Because both checks hold, the program runs through to the final message.

lines.text: The rule that a robot pet burns two battery points per minute of walking lives here, so a 30-minute walk demands 60 points.
The method answers with True or False rather than printing anything, which is exactly what makes it easy to test.
Rover starts with 85 battery points, comfortably above the 60 a half-hour walk costs, so he is the pet we expect to pass.

lines.code: assert rover.can_walk(30) == True, "Rover should be able to walk for 30 minutes"
lines.text: An assert states something you believe must be true: if the expression is true the line does nothing at all, and if it is false Python stops the program and shows the message after the comma.

lines.code: assert beep.can_walk(30) == False, "Beep should not be able to walk for 30 minutes"
lines.text: A good test suite checks the negative case too; Beep's 45 points fall short of 60, so can_walk must say no.
Reaching this line is the whole signal of success, because any failing assert would have halted the program before it.

lines.text: A test class inherits from unittest.TestCase, which is what gives you the assert methods and lets the test runner discover the class.
setUp runs before every single test method, so each test gets its own freshly built pet and no test can be affected by changes another test made.
Every test method's name must begin with test_, or unittest will silently skip it — this is the most common reason a beginner's test "passes" without running.
assertIn checks that the name appears somewhere inside the returned text, which is more robust than demanding the whole sentence match exactly.
Asserting what should not be there catches a real bug: a talent hard-coded to one name would still pass the earlier tests but fail here.
This hands control to the test runner, which finds every test_ method in the file, runs them, and prints a dot per pass along with a summary.

lines.text: The constructor is untouched, so every test that only checks the stored attributes still passes; that is why just two of the four tests fail rather than all of them.
The mood is still stored on the object, but show_talent no longer looks at it. Data can sit on an object completely unused, and nothing about running the program tells you that happened.
This is the sabotage. Every pet now reports the same talent, and because there are no {} placeholders left, the f prefix does nothing at all here.

Printing a pet's talent still looks plausible on screen, so a human skim would not catch the bug. The assertions in the test file compare against the exact expected sentence, which is what makes the failure visible; restore the original return once you have seen it.

examples.title: Unit Tests that Change State
examples.prompt: Create a battery for the robot pet and protect it so it does not go below 0 or above 100
response: return f"{self.name} performs a generic trick!"

explanation.summary: This version of RobotPet keeps the battery level in a property, so every attempt to set it is checked first and forced into the range 0 to 100. The charge() method simply adds to the battery and lets that check do the clamping.

lines.text: Even here in the constructor the assignment goes through the property setter, so a robot pet created with a battery of 150 or -20 is corrected immediately rather than starting out invalid.
This decorator marks the method below it as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to self.battery, which is what lets the class guard the value instead of trusting the caller.
Anything above full charge is capped at 100, which is the behaviour the unit test in the next exercise will check by charging a pet well past full.

The real number lives in the private attribute _battery with an underscore; the property named battery is the guarded doorway in front of it, and mixing the two names up is the easiest mistake to make here.
Because += reads the property and then assigns back to it, charge() gets the clamping for free and needs no bounds checking of its own.

examples.title: Unit Tests that Change State
examples.prompt: Write a unit test to test the charge method

explanation.summary: These four test methods check the RobotPet charge method. Each one sets the battery to a known starting value, charges it by some amount, then asserts the battery ended up where it should.

lines.text: Because we cannot know what the battery starts at, the test sets it deliberately. Fixing the starting value is what turns a guess into a repeatable test scenario.
With a start of 50 and a charge of 20, the only correct answer is 70, so a single assertEqual is enough to prove the charging arithmetic works.
This test is aimed at the battery setter rather than the charge method: 90 plus 50 would be 140, and the setter must clamp it to 100.
A negative charge is how the pet drains its battery, so the same method is tested in the opposite direction.

The mirror image of the cap test — draining 50 from a battery of 10 must stop at 0 instead of going negative. Testing both boundaries is how you know the setter protects the battery in both directions.

import unittest

FILENAME = "implementing_a_new_feature_and_testing_it.py"

# The printed test file uses "..." to stand for the tests shown earlier in the
# chapter. Swap that placeholder for a real statement so the file can be run.
with open(FILENAME, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    source = handle.read().replace("\u2026", "pass")

namespace = {"__name__": "printed_tests", "__file__": FILENAME}
exec(compile(source, FILENAME, "exec"), namespace)

loader = unittest.TestLoader()
suite = unittest.TestSuite()
for value in list(namespace.values()):
    if isinstance(value, type) and issubclass(value, unittest.TestCase):
        suite.addTests(loader.loadTestsFromTestCase(value))

unittest.TextTestRunner(verbosity=2).run(suite)

lines.text: Assigning to self.battery in the constructor runs the property setter, not a plain attribute assignment, so a pet created with battery=150 or battery=-5 is corrected before anything else touches it.
The setter stores the cleaned-up number in the private _battery attribute; this is where the two new unit tests for the battery bounds aim their assertions.

lines.code: from pet_talents import RobotPet, RobotCat, RobotBird, RobotDog

The ellipsis stands for the setUp method and the earlier tests that were already in each test class; the printed page shows only the new speak tests being added. Because of it, this file as printed is a fragment rather than a program you can run.
Rather than draining the battery through gameplay, the test sets the attribute straight to a value below 30 to put the pet in exactly the state the branch needs.
Testing the happy message means also raising the battery on the next line, because a flat battery takes priority inside speak and would hide the mood message entirely.
assertIn checks that the returned message contains a word, not that it matches character for character, so the test still passes if you later reword the greeting around it.
Each pet type repeats this test to confirm the message identifies the pet, which is the easiest detail to lose when four classes each write their own version of speak.

'''
